newsitem.title: India: Last bodies pulled from India plane crash site.
newsitem.headline: Last bodies pulled from India plane crash site.

text.p: The last two bodies of the 349 victims of the world's deadliest mid-air collision have been recovered from the debris of a Saudi jumbo jet, Indian officials said on Monday.
Two bodies were pulled on Sunday from the wreckage of the Saudi Airlines Boeing 747 which crashed with 312 people last Tuesday after colliding with a Kazakh cargo plane.

An official in Charkhi Dadri town, 80 km (50 miles) west of New Delhi, said the bodies of two Indian nationals were the last remaining victims from the Saudi aircraft, and that they were being taken to their home towns in northern India.
Passports and some personal belongings were found near the bodies, helping emergency workers identify the victims, the Press Trust of India (PTI) said.
The bodies of all 37 people from the Kazakh Ilyushin IL-76 freighter were found shortly after the accident.
Officials said 58 unidentified bodies from the crash would be cremated or buried on Tuesday, PTI said.
A team of Kazakh officials helping their Indian counterparts investigate the crash said they had found no evidence to indicate the cause of the collision.
"No, no, we have found nothing," Kazakhstan's acting Director-General of Civil Aviation, Bekpulat Salimov, the spokesman for the 15-member Kazakh team, told Reuters.
Salimov said the team planned to make a request on Tuesday to the Indian judge leading the probe to hand over the black box flight recorders of the Kazakh aircraft for decoding.

"We have highly qualified people, good laboratories and workshops," he added. "The decoding can be done in Moscow, or in Uzbekistan, where it was manufactured, or in Kazakhstan, where it was registered."
Salimov said the Ilyushin was four years old and had logged just over 2,500 flying hours. He said it had no history of maintenance or spare parts problems.

Speculation over the cause of the crash has ranged from fears that the Kazakh pilot did not understand English to the possibility of confusion over the aircraft's height because it was not calibrated in feet.
Pilots in the former Soviet Union use the metric system.

Salimov said the Kazakh pilot was fluent in English, the vernacular of international aviation. "(He) was an experienced pilot," Salimov said. "He had flown more than about 10,000 hours. He spoke English. He was very good.

"We took from the crash from the cockpit, two feet-meters from the Ilyushin, one was situated in front of the captain, the second one in front of the navigator, where both captain and navigator can easily see what was the level of flight."
Most passengers on the Saudi plane were Indian nationals returning to jobs in the Gulf or going there to seek work.
The mid-air disaster has focused harsh attention on India's flight safety record.
The Civil Aviation Ministry has ordered an investigation into delays in the completion of a plan to modernise air traffic control systems in Delhi and Bombay airports, the PTI said.
Sophisticated equipment designed by Raytheon Co of the United States was due to be operational six months ago but has been held up by technical glitches.
It could have given controllers in Delhi the information they needed to warn the Saudi and Kazakh planes that they were headed towards disaster if it had been in operation.
Officials now expect the system to be on line early in 1997.
